**Judith Krantz** (née **Tarcher**; January 9, 1928 – June 22, 2019) was an American magazine writer, fashion editor, and novelist. Her first novel _[Scruples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scruples\_(novel) "Scruples (novel)")_ (1978) was a _[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_Best\_Seller\_list "The New York Times Best Seller list")_[best-seller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Best_Seller_list "The New York Times Best Seller list")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-1) and was translated into 50 languages. _Scruples_, which describes the glamorous and affluent world of high fashion in [Beverly Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Hills "Beverly Hills"), California, helped define a new sub-genre of the [romance novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_novel "Romance novel")— the [bonkbuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonkbuster "Bonkbuster") or "sex-and-shopping" novel.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-bloom-2) She also became a "celebrity author" through her extensive touring and promotion.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-ham-3) Her later books included _[Princess Daisy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess\_Daisy\_(novel) "Princess Daisy (novel)")_ (1980), _[Mistral's Daughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistral's\_Daughter "Mistral's Daughter")_ (1982) _[Till We Meet Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Till\_We\_Meet\_Again\_(novel) "Till We Meet Again (novel)")_ (1988), _Dazzle_ (1990), and _Spring Collection_ (1996).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-4) Her autobiography, _Sex and Shopping: The Confessions of a Nice Jewish Girl_, was published in 2000.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-sex-5)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

### Early years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years")]

Judith Bluma-Gittel Tarcher was born on January 9, 1928,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-6) in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), the daughter of Mary (Braeger), a [Lithuanian-born](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuanian_Americans "Lithuanian Americans") attorney, and Jack D. Tarcher, an advertising executive.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-7) Her family was [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-8) The "youngest, smartest, and shortest girl" in her year,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-well-9) she graduated from the [Birch Wathen School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Birch_Wathen_Lenox_School "The Birch Wathen Lenox School") at age 16. Krantz then enrolled at [Wellesley College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellesley_College "Wellesley College").

Krantz told _[The Boston Globe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boston\_Globe "The Boston Globe")_ in 1982 that she attended Wellesley with three goals: to date, to read every novel in the library, and to graduate.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-well-9) "Torchy", as her dormmates named her, held the dorm dating record as the only one to have 13 consecutive dates with 13 different men. Her grades were not as impressive as her extracurricular activities.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-well-9) Krantz earned one A-plus in English, but had a B− average in her major and C average in everything else. Krantz had the opportunity to improve her marks when she took a short-story class during her sophomore year. Although the professor enjoyed her writing, he refused to give her an A because she had poor spelling, and he thought the B would teach her a lesson. Krantz claims to have learned the lesson well—she did not write fiction again for 31 years.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-sex-5)

After graduating from Wellesley in 1948, Krantz moved to Paris, where she worked in fashion [public relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_relations "Public relations"). She enjoyed attending elegant parties, borrowing [couture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haute_couture "Haute couture") gowns, and meeting prominent people such as [Marlene Dietrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlene_Dietrich "Marlene Dietrich"), [Orson Welles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orson_Welles "Orson Welles") and [Hubert de Givenchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_de_Givenchy "Hubert de Givenchy").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-well-9)

#### Magazines

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Magazines")]

The following year, Krantz returned to New York City, where began a career in magazine journalism. She worked in the fiction department at _[Good Housekeeping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good\_Housekeeping "Good Housekeeping")_ before being promoted to fashion editor and having the opportunity to write several articles for the magazine.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-book-10)

In 1953 Krantz attended a Fourth of July party hosted by her high school friend, [Barbara Walters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Walters "Barbara Walters"). There she met the future film and television producer [Steve Krantz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Krantz "Steve Krantz").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-steveobit-11) The two were married the following year, on February 19, 1954. Three years later, she gave birth to their first son, and she gave up her full-time job, choosing instead to write part-time from home.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-book-10) She wrote many freelance articles for _[Maclean's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maclean's "Maclean's")_, _[McCall's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCall's "McCall's")_, _[Ladies' Home Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladies'\_Home\_Journal "Ladies' Home Journal")_, and _[Cosmopolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmopolitan\_(magazine) "Cosmopolitan (magazine)")._ Her best-known article was "The Myth of the Multiple Orgasm", which was published in _Cosmopolitan._[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-12) Her magazine career gave Krantz an opportunity to interview many prominent women.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-book-10)

### Novels

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Novels")]

In 1976, Krantz's husband decided to take flying lessons. Despite Krantz having a fear of flying, she joined the flying lessons with him, after which her fears were subdued. Subsequently, she wrote fiction for the first time since college. Although her husband had been insisting for years that she was a natural storyteller, Krantz believed that she was writing the book simply to prove to him that she was not able to write good fiction.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-steveobit-11)

She completed her first novel, _[Scruples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scruples\_(novel) "Scruples (novel)")_, nine months later. The year it was published, 1978, Krantz turned 50. The books were not copyrighted under her own name but by Steve Krantz Productions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-steveobit-11)_Scruples_ reached the number one spot on [_The New York Times_ bestseller list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Best_Seller_list "The New York Times Best Seller list"). There were two sequels: _Scruples Two_ (1992) and _Lovers_ (1994).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-ham-3)

Her second novel, _[Princess Daisy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess\_Daisy\_(novel) "Princess Daisy (novel)")_, followed in 1980 and netted her $5 million before its publication. It also became a number one best seller, with the paperback rights selling for a then-record $3.2 million.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-fraser-13) It concerns the fabulously wealthy and glamorous Daisy, daughter of a Russian prince, who has to confront and overcome many harsh realities. The book is notable for having received one of the most scathing reviews ever written, by [Clive James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_James "Clive James").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-14) Krantz continued her run of success with _Mistral's Daughter_ (1982) (a multi-generational saga) and _[I'll Take Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'll\_Take\_Manhattan "I'll Take Manhattan")_ (1986), (about writer and socialite Maxi Amberville, a thinly disguised portrait of the author).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-ham-3) Mistral's Daughter went beyond the formula (with only four sex scenes, all at the beginning of the book), delving into women's empowerment, art, Jewish spirituality, and the persecution of Jewish people in France during World War II.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-15)_[Till We Meet Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Till\_We\_Meet\_Again\_(novel) "Till We Meet Again (novel)")_ (1988) which starts in the music halls of 1910s Paris and continues on until after the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), was the last to make the [annual top ten bestseller lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Weekly_list_of_bestselling_novels_in_the_United_States_in_the_1980s "Publishers Weekly list of bestselling novels in the United States in the 1980s"), though the later novels continued to be popular.

_Spring Collection_ (1996) returns to the world of fashion, while _The Jewels of Tessa Kent_ (1998) explores mother-daughter relationships; Krantz reportedly had a difficult relationship with her own mother.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-16) She retired from writing that year at the age of 70, saying she had nothing left to say to her readers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-bloom-2) Over 80 million copies of her books are in print in over 50 languages. Seven of her novels have also been adapted for television (as either films or mini-series), with her husband having served as executive producer for some of them.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-fraser-13) She also wrote one original mini-series for television, _Judith Krantz's "Secrets"_, in 1992.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-17)

### Family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Family")]

Krantz served on the advisory board of [Compassion & Choices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compassion_&_Choices "Compassion & Choices"), an organization dedicated to providing choices for the dying.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-compassion-18) In 2006, she joined the Board of the [Los Angeles Music Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Music_Center "Los Angeles Music Center").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-music-19)

Krantz's husband, Steve Krantz, died in 2007 of pneumonia. The couple had two sons, [Tony Krantz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Krantz "Tony Krantz") and Nicholas Krantz, both of whom reside in the Los Angeles area.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-steveobit-11) Krantz was the sister-in-law of children's entertainer and television host [Shari Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shari_Lewis "Shari Lewis"), who was married to Krantz's brother, [Jeremy P. Tarcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TarcherPerigee "TarcherPerigee"), publisher of nonfiction books on health, psychology and New Age spirituality. Jeremy's daughter, Krantz's niece, is entertainer [Mallory Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mallory_Lewis "Mallory Lewis"). Krantz has two grandchildren, Michael Krantz and Kate Krantz.

### Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Death")]

Krantz died on June 22, 2019, at her home in the [Bel Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel_Air,_Los_Angeles "Bel Air, Los Angeles") neighborhood of Los Angeles.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-20)

===Early years===

Judith Bluma-Gittel Tarcher was born on January 9, 1928,<ref>{{cite news|url= https://www.upi.com/Top_News/2020/01/09/UPI-Almanac-for-Thursday-Jan-9-2020/6871578415895/|title= UPI Almanac for Thursday, Jan. 9, 2020|work=[[United Press International]]| date= January 9, 2020|access-date=January 16, 2020 |archive-date= January 15, 2020|archive-url= https://archive.today/20200115192229/https://www.upi.com/Top_News/2020/01/09/UPI-Almanac-for-Thursday-Jan-9-2020/6871578415895/|url-status=live|quote=…author Judith Krantz in 1928}}</ref> in [[New York City]], the daughter of Mary (Braeger), a [[Lithuanian Americans|Lithuanian-born]] attorney, and Jack D. Tarcher, an advertising executive.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/judith-krantz-dead-best-selling-author-journalist-dies-at-91-1220487|title=Judith Krantz, Best-Selling Author and Journalist, Dies at 91|website=The Hollywood Reporter|date=June 23, 2019 |access-date=June 24, 2019}}</ref> Her family was [[Jews|Jewish]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/06/23/us/judith-krantz-obit/index.html|title=Judith Krantz, romance novelist, dies at 91|first1=Leah|last1=Asmelash|first2=Melissa|last2=Gray|website=CNN|date=June 23, 2019 |access-date=June 24, 2019}}</ref> The "youngest, smartest, and shortest girl" in her year,<ref name="well">{{cite web| last =Ruark| first =Liz| title =Person of the Week: Judith Tarcher Krantz '48| publisher =Wellesley| date =February 12, 2001| url =http://www.wellesley.edu/Anniversary/krantz.html| access-date =February 6, 2007| url-status =dead| archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20060901234531/http://www.wellesley.edu/Anniversary/krantz.html| archive-date =September 1, 2006}}</ref> she graduated from the [[The Birch Wathen Lenox School|Birch Wathen School]] at age 16. Krantz then enrolled at [[Wellesley College]].

  

Krantz told ''[[The Boston Globe]]'' in 1982 that she attended Wellesley with three goals: to date, to read every novel in the library, and to graduate.<ref name="well"/> "Torchy", as her dormmates named her, held the dorm dating record as the only one to have 13 consecutive dates with 13 different men. Her grades were not as impressive as her extracurricular activities.<ref name="well"/> Krantz earned one A-plus in English, but had a B− average in her major and C average in everything else. Krantz had the opportunity to improve her marks when she took a short-story class during her sophomore year. Although the professor enjoyed her writing, he refused to give her an A because she had poor spelling, and he thought the B would teach her a lesson. Krantz claims to have learned the lesson well—she did not write fiction again for 31 years.<ref name="sex"/>

  

After graduating from Wellesley in 1948, Krantz moved to Paris, where she worked in fashion [[public relations]]. She enjoyed attending elegant parties, borrowing [[haute couture|couture]] gowns, and meeting prominent people such as [[Marlene Dietrich]], [[Orson Welles]] and [[Hubert de Givenchy]].<ref name="well"/>

  

====Magazines====

The following year, Krantz returned to New York City, where began a career in magazine journalism. She worked in the fiction department at ''[[Good Housekeeping]]'' before being promoted to fashion editor and having the opportunity to write several articles for the magazine.<ref name="book">{{cite web| last =Huseby| first =Sandy| title =Judith Krantz: Life is even better than fiction| publisher =Book Page| year =2000| url =http://www.bookpage.com/0005bp/judith_krantz.html| access-date =February 6, 2007| url-status =dead| archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20070409061754/http://www.bookpage.com/0005bp/judith_krantz.html| archive-date =April 9, 2007}}</ref>

  

In 1953 Krantz attended a Fourth of July party hosted by her high school friend, [[Barbara Walters]]. There she met the future film and television producer [[Steve Krantz]].<ref name="steveobit">

{{cite web | last = Martin | first =Douglas | title =Steve Krantz, 83, Maker of TV Mini-Series, Dies | work =New York Times

| date =January 12, 2007 | url =https://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/12/obituaries/12krantz.html?ex=1326258000&en=f1844dbcdaa0605d&ei=5088&partner=rssnyt&emc=rss

| access-date = February 6, 2007 }}</ref> The two were married the following year, on February 19, 1954. Three years later, she gave birth to their first son, and she gave up her full-time job, choosing instead to write part-time from home.<ref name="book"/> She wrote many freelance articles for ''[[Maclean's]]'', ''[[McCall's]]'', ''[[Ladies' Home Journal]]'', and ''[[Cosmopolitan (magazine)|Cosmopolitan]].'' Her best-known article was "The Myth of the Multiple Orgasm", which was published in ''Cosmopolitan.''<ref>Mansfield, Stephanie. [https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1986/05/20/steamy-sex-shop-talk-judith-krantz/cb92a7c2-91a5-4a43-9e8a-4292fbd1a83e/'Steamy Sex Shop Talk, Judith Krantz'], in ''The Washington Post,'' 20 May 1986</ref> Her magazine career gave Krantz an opportunity to interview many prominent women.<ref name="book"/>

### Novels

In 1976, Krantz's husband decided to take flying lessons. Despite Krantz having a fear of flying, she joined the flying lessons with him, after which her fears were subdued. Subsequently, she wrote fiction for the first time since college. Although her husband had been insisting for years that she was a natural storyteller, Krantz believed that she was writing the book simply to prove to him that she was not able to write good fiction.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#)!Image 125

She completed her first novel, _![Image 126](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith\_Krantz&action=edit&section=2)[![Image 127](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith\_Krantz&action=edit&section=2)Scruples![Image 128](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith\_Krantz&action=edit&section=2)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scruples\_(novel) "Scruples (novel)")![Image 129](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith\_Krantz&action=edit&section=2)_, nine months later. The year it was published, 1978, Krantz turned 50. The books were not copyrighted under her own name but by Steve Krantz Productions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#)_Scruples_ reached the number one spot on !Image 130![Image 131_The New York Times_ bestseller list!Image 132](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Best_Seller_list "The New York Times Best Seller list")!Image 133. There were two sequels: _Scruples Two_ (1992) and _Lovers_ (1994).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#)!Image 134

Her second novel, _![Image 135](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith\_Krantz&action=edit&section=2)[![Image 136](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith\_Krantz&action=edit&section=2)Princess Daisy![Image 137](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith\_Krantz&action=edit&section=2)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess\_Daisy\_(novel) "Princess Daisy (novel)")![Image 138](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith\_Krantz&action=edit&section=2)_, followed in 1980 and netted her $5 million before its publication. It also became a number one best seller, with the paperback rights selling for a then-record $3.2 million.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#) It concerns the fabulously wealthy and glamorous Daisy, daughter of a Russian prince, who has to confront and overcome many harsh realities. The book is notable for having received one of the most scathing reviews ever written, by !Image 139![Image 140Clive James!Image 141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_James "Clive James")!Image 142.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#) Krantz continued her run of success with _Mistral's Daughter_ (1982) (a multi-generational saga) and author).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#) Mistral's Daughter went beyond the formula (with only four sex scenes, all at the beginning of the book), delving into women's empowerment, art, Jewish spirituality, and the persecution of Jewish people in France during World War _Spring Collection_ (1996) returns to the world of fashion, while _The Jewels of Tessa Kent_ (1998) explores mother-daughter relationships; Krantz reportedly had a difficult relationship with her own mother.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#) She retired from writing that year at the age of 70, saying she had nothing left to say to her readers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#) Over 80 million copies of her books are in print in over 50 languages. Seven of her novels have also been adapted for television (as either films or mini-series), with her husband having served as executive producer for some of them.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#) She also wrote one original mini-series for television, _Judith Krantz's "Secrets"_, in 1992.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#)!Image 159

### Family

Krantz served on the advisory board of !Image 160![Image 161Compassion & Choices!Image 162](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compassion_&_Choices "Compassion & Choices")!Image 163, an organization dedicated to providing choices for the dying.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#) In 2006, she joined the Board of the !Image 164![Image 165Los Angeles Music Center!Image 166](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Music_Center "Los Angeles Music Center")!Image 167.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#)!Image 168

Krantz's husband, Steve Krantz, died in 2007 of pneumonia. The couple had two sons, !Image 169![Image 170Tony Krantz!Image 171](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Krantz "Tony Krantz")!Image 172 and Nicholas Krantz, both of whom reside in the Los Angeles area.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2#) Krantz was the sister-in-law of children's entertainer and television host !Image 173![Image 174Shari Lewis!Image 175](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shari_Lewis "Shari Lewis")!Image 176, who was married to Krantz's brother, !Image 177![Image 178Jeremy P. Tarcher!Image 179](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TarcherPerigee "TarcherPerigee")!Image 180, publisher of nonfiction books on health, psychology and New Age spirituality. Jeremy's daughter, Krantz's niece, is entertainer !Image 181![Image 182Mallory Lewis!Image 183](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mallory_Lewis "Mallory Lewis")!Image 184. Krantz has two grandchildren, Michael Krantz and Kate Krantz.

Tarcher, an advertising executive.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/judith-krantz-dead-best-selling-author-journalist-dies-at-91-1220487|title=Judith Krantz, Best-Selling Author and Journalist, Dies at 91|website=The Hollywood Reporter|date=June 23, 2019 |access-date=June 24, 2019}}</ref> Her family was [[Jews|Jewish]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/06/23/us/judith-krantz-obit/index.html|title=Judith Krantz, romance novelist, dies at 91|first1=Leah|last1=Asmelash|first2=Melissa|last2=Gray|website=CNN|date=June 23, 2019 |access-date=June 24, 2019}}</ref> The "youngest, smartest, and shortest girl" in her year,<ref name="well">{{cite web| last =Ruark| first =Liz| title =Person of the Week: Judith Tarcher Krantz '48| publisher =Wellesley| date =February 12, 2001| url =http://www.wellesley.edu/Anniversary/krantz.html| access-date =February 6, 2007| url-status =dead| archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20060901234531/http://www.wellesley.edu/Anniversary/krantz.html| archive-date =September 1, 2006}}</ref> she graduated from the [[The Birch Wathen Lenox School|Birch Wathen School]] at age 16. Krantz then enrolled at [[Wellesley College]].

  

Krantz told ''[[The Boston Globe]]'' in 1982 that she attended Wellesley with three goals: to date, to read every novel in the library, and to graduate.<ref name="well"/> "Torchy", as her dormmates named her, held the dorm dating record as the only one to have 13 consecutive dates with 13 different men. Her grades were not as impressive as her extracurricular activities.<ref name="well"/> Krantz earned one A-plus in English, but had a B− average in her major and C average in everything else. Krantz had the opportunity to improve her marks when she took a short-story class during her sophomore year. Although the professor enjoyed her writing, he refused to give her an A because she had poor spelling, and he thought the B would teach her a lesson. Krantz claims to have learned the lesson well—she did not write fiction again for 31 years.<ref name="sex"/>

  

After graduating from Wellesley in 1948, Krantz moved to Paris, where she worked in fashion [[public relations]]. She enjoyed attending elegant parties, borrowing [[haute couture|couture]] gowns, and meeting prominent people such as [[Marlene Dietrich]], [[Orson Welles]] and [[Hubert de Givenchy]].<ref name="well"/>

  

====Magazines====

The following year, Krantz returned to New York City, where began a career in magazine journalism. She worked in the fiction department at ''[[Good Housekeeping]]'' before being promoted to fashion editor and having the opportunity to write several articles for the magazine.<ref name="book">{{cite web| last =Huseby| first =Sandy| title =Judith Krantz: Life is even better than fiction| publisher =Book Page| year =2000| url =http://www.bookpage.com/0005bp/judith_krantz.html| access-date =February 6, 2007| url-status =dead| archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20070409061754/http://www.bookpage.com/0005bp/judith_krantz.html| archive-date =April 9, 2007}}</ref>

  

In 1953 Krantz attended a Fourth of July party hosted by her high school friend, [[Barbara Walters]]. There she met the future film and television producer [[Steve Krantz]].<ref name="steveobit">

{{cite web | last = Martin | first =Douglas | title =Steve Krantz, 83, Maker of TV Mini-Series, Dies | work =New York Times

| date =January 12, 2007 | url =https://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/12/obituaries/12krantz.html?ex=1326258000&en=f1844dbcdaa0605d&ei=5088&partner=rssnyt&emc=rss

| access-date = February 6, 2007 }}</ref> The two were married the following year, on February 19, 1954. Three years later, she gave birth to their first son, and she gave up her full-time job, choosing instead to write part-time from home.<ref name="book"/> She wrote many freelance articles for ''[[Maclean's]]'', ''[[McCall's]]'', ''[[Ladies' Home Journal]]'', and ''[[Cosmopolitan (magazine)|Cosmopolitan]].'' Her best-known article was "The Myth of the Multiple Orgasm", which was published in ''Cosmopolitan.''<ref>Mansfield, Stephanie. [https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1986/05/20/steamy-sex-shop-talk-judith-krantz/cb92a7c2-91a5-4a43-9e8a-4292fbd1a83e/'Steamy Sex Shop Talk, Judith Krantz'], in ''The Washington Post,'' 20 May 1986</ref> Her magazine career gave Krantz an opportunity to interview many prominent women.<ref name="book"/>

**Judith Krantz** (née **Tarcher**; January 9, 1928 – June 22, 2019) was an American magazine writer, fashion editor, and novelist. Her first novel _[Scruples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scruples\_(novel) "Scruples (novel)")_ (1978) was a _[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_Best\_Seller\_list "The New York Times Best Seller list")_[best-seller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Best_Seller_list "The New York Times Best Seller list")[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-1) and was translated into 50 languages. _Scruples_, which describes the glamorous and affluent world of high fashion in [Beverly Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Hills "Beverly Hills"), California, helped define a new sub-genre of the [romance novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_novel "Romance novel")— the [bonkbuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonkbuster "Bonkbuster") or "sex-and-shopping" novel.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-bloom-2) She also became a "celebrity author" through her extensive touring and promotion.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-ham-3) Her later books included _[Princess Daisy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess\_Daisy\_(novel) "Princess Daisy (novel)")_ (1980), _[Mistral's Daughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistral's\_Daughter "Mistral's Daughter")_ (1982) _[Till We Meet Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Till\_We\_Meet\_Again\_(novel) "Till We Meet Again (novel)")_ (1988), _Dazzle_ (1990), and _Spring Collection_ (1996).[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-4) Her autobiography, _Sex and Shopping: The Confessions of a Nice Jewish Girl_, was published in 2000.[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-sex-5)

## Biography

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

### Early years

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years")]

Judith Bluma-Gittel Tarcher was born on January 9, 1928,[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-6) in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), the daughter of Mary (Braeger), a [Lithuanian-born](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuanian_Americans "Lithuanian Americans") attorney, and Jack D. Tarcher, an advertising executive.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-7) Her family was [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews").[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-8) The "youngest, smartest, and shortest girl" in her year,[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-well-9) she graduated from the [Birch Wathen School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Birch_Wathen_Lenox_School "The Birch Wathen Lenox School") at age 16. Krantz then enrolled at [Wellesley College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellesley_College "Wellesley College").

Krantz told _[The Boston Globe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boston\_Globe "The Boston Globe")_ in 1982 that she attended Wellesley with three goals: to date, to read every novel in the library, and to graduate.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-well-9) "Torchy", as her dormmates named her, held the dorm dating record as the only one to have 13 consecutive dates with 13 different men. Her grades were not as impressive as her extracurricular activities.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-well-9) Krantz earned one A-plus in English, but had a B− average in her major and C average in everything else. Krantz had the opportunity to improve her marks when she took a short-story class during her sophomore year. Although the professor enjoyed her writing, he refused to give her an A because she had poor spelling, and he thought the B would teach her a lesson. Krantz claims to have learned the lesson well—she did not write fiction again for 31 years.[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-sex-5)

After graduating from Wellesley in 1948, Krantz moved to Paris, where she worked in fashion [public relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_relations "Public relations"). She enjoyed attending elegant parties, borrowing [couture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haute_couture "Haute couture") gowns, and meeting prominent people such as [Marlene Dietrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlene_Dietrich "Marlene Dietrich"), [Orson Welles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orson_Welles "Orson Welles") and [Hubert de Givenchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_de_Givenchy "Hubert de Givenchy").[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-well-9)

#### Magazines

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Magazines")]

The following year, Krantz returned to New York City, where began a career in magazine journalism. She worked in the fiction department at _[Good Housekeeping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good\_Housekeeping "Good Housekeeping")_ before being promoted to fashion editor and having the opportunity to write several articles for the magazine.[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-book-10)

In 1953 Krantz attended a Fourth of July party hosted by her high school friend, [Barbara Walters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Walters "Barbara Walters"). There she met the future film and television producer [Steve Krantz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Krantz "Steve Krantz").[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-steveobit-11) The two were married the following year, on February 19, 1954. Three years later, she gave birth to their first son, and she gave up her full-time job, choosing instead to write part-time from home.[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-book-10) She wrote many freelance articles for _[Maclean's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maclean's "Maclean's")_, _[McCall's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCall's "McCall's")_, _[Ladies' Home Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladies'\_Home\_Journal "Ladies' Home Journal")_, and _[Cosmopolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmopolitan\_(magazine) "Cosmopolitan (magazine)")._ Her best-known article was "The Myth of the Multiple Orgasm", which was published in _Cosmopolitan._[[12]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-12) Her magazine career gave Krantz an opportunity to interview many prominent women.[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-book-10)

### Novels

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Novels")]

In 1976, Krantz's husband decided to take flying lessons. Despite Krantz having a fear of flying, she joined the flying lessons with him, after which her fears were subdued. Subsequently, she wrote fiction for the first time since college. Although her husband had been insisting for years that she was a natural storyteller, Krantz believed that she was writing the book simply to prove to him that she was not able to write good fiction.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-steveobit-11)

She completed her first novel, _[Scruples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scruples\_(novel) "Scruples (novel)")_, nine months later. The year it was published, 1978, Krantz turned 50. The books were not copyrighted under her own name but by Steve Krantz Productions.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-steveobit-11)_Scruples_ reached the number one spot on [_The New York Times_ bestseller list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Best_Seller_list "The New York Times Best Seller list"). There were two sequels: _Scruples Two_ (1992) and _Lovers_ (1994).[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-ham-3)

Her second novel, _[Princess Daisy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess\_Daisy\_(novel) "Princess Daisy (novel)")_, followed in 1980 and netted her $5 million before its publication. It also became a number one best seller, with the paperback rights selling for a then-record $3.2 million.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-fraser-13) It concerns the fabulously wealthy and glamorous Daisy, daughter of a Russian prince, who has to confront and overcome many harsh realities. The book is notable for having received one of the most scathing reviews ever written, by [Clive James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_James "Clive James").[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-14) Krantz continued her run of success with _Mistral's Daughter_ (1982) (a multi-generational saga) and _[I'll Take Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'll\_Take\_Manhattan "I'll Take Manhattan")_ (1986), (about writer and socialite Maxi Amberville, a thinly disguised portrait of the author).[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-ham-3) Mistral's Daughter went beyond the formula (with only four sex scenes, all at the beginning of the book), delving into women's empowerment, art, Jewish spirituality, and the persecution of Jewish people in France during World War II.[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-15)_[Till We Meet Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Till\_We\_Meet\_Again\_(novel) "Till We Meet Again (novel)")_ (1988) which starts in the music halls of 1910s Paris and continues on until after the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), was the last to make the [annual top ten bestseller lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Weekly_list_of_bestselling_novels_in_the_United_States_in_the_1980s "Publishers Weekly list of bestselling novels in the United States in the 1980s"), though the later novels continued to be popular.

_Spring Collection_ (1996) returns to the world of fashion, while _The Jewels of Tessa Kent_ (1998) explores mother-daughter relationships; Krantz reportedly had a difficult relationship with her own mother.[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-16) She retired from writing that year at the age of 70, saying she had nothing left to say to her readers.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-bloom-2) Over 80 million copies of her books are in print in over 50 languages. Seven of her novels have also been adapted for television (as either films or mini-series), with her husband having served as executive producer for some of them.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-fraser-13) She also wrote one original mini-series for television, _Judith Krantz's "Secrets"_, in 1992.[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-17)

### Family

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Family")]

Krantz served on the advisory board of [Compassion & Choices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compassion_&_Choices "Compassion & Choices"), an organization dedicated to providing choices for the dying.[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-compassion-18) In 2006, she joined the Board of the [Los Angeles Music Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Music_Center "Los Angeles Music Center").[[19]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-music-19)

Krantz's husband, Steve Krantz, died in 2007 of pneumonia. The couple had two sons, [Tony Krantz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Krantz "Tony Krantz") and Nicholas Krantz, both of whom reside in the Los Angeles area.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-steveobit-11) Krantz was the sister-in-law of children's entertainer and television host [Shari Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shari_Lewis "Shari Lewis"), who was married to Krantz's brother, [Jeremy P. Tarcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TarcherPerigee "TarcherPerigee"), publisher of nonfiction books on health, psychology and New Age spirituality. Jeremy's daughter, Krantz's niece, is entertainer [Mallory Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mallory_Lewis "Mallory Lewis"). Krantz has two grandchildren, Michael Krantz and Kate Krantz.

### Death

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Death")]

Krantz died on June 22, 2019, at her home in the [Bel Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel_Air,_Los_Angeles "Bel Air, Los Angeles") neighborhood of Los Angeles.[[20]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-20)

**Judith Krantz** (née **Tarcher**; January 9, 1928 – June 22, 2019) was an American magazine writer, fashion editor, and novelist. Her first novel _[Scruples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scruples\_(novel) "Scruples (novel)")_ (1978) was a _[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_Best\_Seller\_list "The New York Times Best Seller list")_[best-seller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Best_Seller_list "The New York Times Best Seller list")[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-1) and was translated into 50 languages. _Scruples_, which describes the glamorous and affluent world of high fashion in [Beverly Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Hills "Beverly Hills"), California, helped define a new sub-genre of the [romance novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_novel "Romance novel")— the [bonkbuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonkbuster "Bonkbuster") or "sex-and-shopping" novel.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-bloom-2) She also became a "celebrity author" through her extensive touring and promotion.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-ham-3) Her later books included _[Princess Daisy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess\_Daisy\_(novel) "Princess Daisy (novel)")_ (1980), _[Mistral's Daughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistral's\_Daughter "Mistral's Daughter")_ (1982) _[Till We Meet Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Till\_We\_Meet\_Again\_(novel) "Till We Meet Again (novel)")_ (1988), _Dazzle_ (1990), and _Spring Collection_ (1996).[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-4) Her autobiography, _Sex and Shopping: The Confessions of a Nice Jewish Girl_, was published in 2000.[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-sex-5)

## Biography

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

### Early years

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years")]

Judith Bluma-Gittel Tarcher was born on January 9, 1928,[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-6) in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), the daughter of Mary (Braeger), a [Lithuanian-born](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuanian_Americans "Lithuanian Americans") attorney, and Jack D. Tarcher, an advertising executive.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-7) Her family was [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews").[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-8) The "youngest, smartest, and shortest girl" in her year,[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-well-9) she graduated from the [Birch Wathen School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Birch_Wathen_Lenox_School "The Birch Wathen Lenox School") at age 16. Krantz then enrolled at [Wellesley College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellesley_College "Wellesley College").

Krantz told _[The Boston Globe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boston\_Globe "The Boston Globe")_ in 1982 that she attended Wellesley with three goals: to date, to read every novel in the library, and to graduate.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-well-9) "Torchy", as her dormmates named her, held the dorm dating record as the only one to have 13 consecutive dates with 13 different men. Her grades were not as impressive as her extracurricular activities.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-well-9) Krantz earned one A-plus in English, but had a B− average in her major and C average in everything else. Krantz had the opportunity to improve her marks when she took a short-story class during her sophomore year. Although the professor enjoyed her writing, he refused to give her an A because she had poor spelling, and he thought the B would teach her a lesson. Krantz claims to have learned the lesson well—she did not write fiction again for 31 years.[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-sex-5)

After graduating from Wellesley in 1948, Krantz moved to Paris, where she worked in fashion [public relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_relations "Public relations"). She enjoyed attending elegant parties, borrowing [couture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haute_couture "Haute couture") gowns, and meeting prominent people such as [Marlene Dietrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlene_Dietrich "Marlene Dietrich"), [Orson Welles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orson_Welles "Orson Welles") and [Hubert de Givenchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_de_Givenchy "Hubert de Givenchy").[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-well-9)

#### Magazines

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Magazines")]

The following year, Krantz returned to New York City, where began a career in magazine journalism. She worked in the fiction department at _[Good Housekeeping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good\_Housekeeping "Good Housekeeping")_ before being promoted to fashion editor and having the opportunity to write several articles for the magazine.[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-book-10)

In 1953 Krantz attended a Fourth of July party hosted by her high school friend, [Barbara Walters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Walters "Barbara Walters"). There she met the future film and television producer [Steve Krantz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Krantz "Steve Krantz").[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-steveobit-11) The two were married the following year, on February 19, 1954. Three years later, she gave birth to their first son, and she gave up her full-time job, choosing instead to write part-time from home.[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-book-10) She wrote many freelance articles for _[Maclean's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maclean's "Maclean's")_, _[McCall's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCall's "McCall's")_, _[Ladies' Home Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladies'\_Home\_Journal "Ladies' Home Journal")_, and _[Cosmopolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmopolitan\_(magazine) "Cosmopolitan (magazine)")._ Her best-known article was "The Myth of the Multiple Orgasm", which was published in _Cosmopolitan._[[12]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-12) Her magazine career gave Krantz an opportunity to interview many prominent women.[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-book-10)

### Novels

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Novels")]

In 1976, Krantz's husband decided to take flying lessons. Despite Krantz having a fear of flying, she joined the flying lessons with him, after which her fears were subdued. Subsequently, she wrote fiction for the first time since college. Although her husband had been insisting for years that she was a natural storyteller, Krantz believed that she was writing the book simply to prove to him that she was not able to write good fiction.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-steveobit-11)

She completed her first novel, _[Scruples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scruples\_(novel) "Scruples (novel)")_, nine months later. The year it was published, 1978, Krantz turned 50. The books were not copyrighted under her own name but by Steve Krantz Productions.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-steveobit-11)_Scruples_ reached the number one spot on [_The New York Times_ bestseller list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Best_Seller_list "The New York Times Best Seller list"). There were two sequels: _Scruples Two_ (1992) and _Lovers_ (1994).[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-ham-3)

Her second novel, _[Princess Daisy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess\_Daisy\_(novel) "Princess Daisy (novel)")_, followed in 1980 and netted her $5 million before its publication. It also became a number one best seller, with the paperback rights selling for a then-record $3.2 million.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-fraser-13) It concerns the fabulously wealthy and glamorous Daisy, daughter of a Russian prince, who has to confront and overcome many harsh realities. The book is notable for having received one of the most scathing reviews ever written, by [Clive James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_James "Clive James").[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-14) Krantz continued her run of success with _Mistral's Daughter_ (1982) (a multi-generational saga) and _[I'll Take Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'll\_Take\_Manhattan "I'll Take Manhattan")_ (1986), (about writer and socialite Maxi Amberville, a thinly disguised portrait of the author).[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-ham-3) Mistral's Daughter went beyond the formula (with only four sex scenes, all at the beginning of the book), delving into women's empowerment, art, Jewish spirituality, and the persecution of Jewish people in France during World War II.[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-15)_[Till We Meet Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Till\_We\_Meet\_Again\_(novel) "Till We Meet Again (novel)")_ (1988) which starts in the music halls of 1910s Paris and continues on until after the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), was the last to make the [annual top ten bestseller lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Weekly_list_of_bestselling_novels_in_the_United_States_in_the_1980s "Publishers Weekly list of bestselling novels in the United States in the 1980s"), though the later novels continued to be popular.

_Spring Collection_ (1996) returns to the world of fashion, while _The Jewels of Tessa Kent_ (1998) explores mother-daughter relationships; Krantz reportedly had a difficult relationship with her own mother.[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-16) She retired from writing that year at the age of 70, saying she had nothing left to say to her readers.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-bloom-2) Over 80 million copies of her books are in print in over 50 languages. Seven of her novels have also been adapted for television (as either films or mini-series), with her husband having served as executive producer for some of them.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-fraser-13) She also wrote one original mini-series for television, _Judith Krantz's "Secrets"_, in 1992.[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-17)

### Family

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Family")]

Krantz served on the advisory board of [Compassion & Choices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compassion_&_Choices "Compassion & Choices"), an organization dedicated to providing choices for the dying.[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-compassion-18) In 2006, she joined the Board of the [Los Angeles Music Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Music_Center "Los Angeles Music Center").[[19]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-music-19)

Krantz's husband, Steve Krantz, died in 2007 of pneumonia. The couple had two sons, [Tony Krantz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Krantz "Tony Krantz") and Nicholas Krantz, both of whom reside in the Los Angeles area.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-steveobit-11) Krantz was the sister-in-law of children's entertainer and television host [Shari Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shari_Lewis "Shari Lewis"), who was married to Krantz's brother, [Jeremy P. Tarcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TarcherPerigee "TarcherPerigee"), publisher of nonfiction books on health, psychology and New Age spirituality. Jeremy's daughter, Krantz's niece, is entertainer [Mallory Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mallory_Lewis "Mallory Lewis"). Krantz has two grandchildren, Michael Krantz and Kate Krantz.

### Death

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Judith_Krantz&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Death")]

Krantz died on June 22, 2019, at her home in the [Bel Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel_Air,_Los_Angeles "Bel Air, Los Angeles") neighborhood of Los Angeles.[[20]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Krantz#cite_note-20)
