### 2015–2020: _Before this World_ and _American Standard_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Taylor&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2015–2020: Before this World and American Standard")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/James-Taylor-Kim_Taylor-2020.jpg/250px-James-Taylor-Kim_Taylor-2020.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James-Taylor-Kim_Taylor-2020.jpg)

Kim and James Taylor in 2020

After a 45-year wait, James earned his first No.1 album on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart with _[Before This World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Before\_This\_World "Before This World")_. The album, which was released on June 16 through [Concord Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Records "Concord Records"), arrived on top the chart of July 4, 2015, more than 45 years after Taylor arrived on the list with _[Sweet Baby James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet\_Baby\_James "Sweet Baby James")_ (on the March 14, 1970, list). The album launched atop the _Billboard_ 200 with 97,000 equivalent album units earned in the week ending June 21, 2015, according to Nielsen Music. Of its start, pure album sales were 96,000 copies sold, Taylor's best debut week for an album since 2002's _October Road_.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-86)

Taylor cancelled his 2017 concert in [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila") as a protest to the extrajudicial killings of suspects in the [Philippine drug war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_drug_war "Philippine drug war").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-87)

In January 2020, Taylor released his audio memoir _Break Shot: My First 21 Years_ on the streaming service [Audible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audible_(service) "Audible (service)").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-:0-88)

Taylor's album _[American Standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Standard\_(James\_Taylor\_album) "American Standard (James Taylor album)")_ was released on February 28, 2020. _American Standard_ debuted at No. 4 on the _Billboard_ 200 albums chart, making Taylor the first act to earn a top 10 album in each of the last six decades.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-Billboard-89) On November 24, 2020, the album was nominated for a [Grammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy "Grammy") in the category of "[Best Traditional Pop Vocal Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Traditional_Pop_Vocal_Album "Best Traditional Pop Vocal Album")".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-90) At the [63rd Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/63rd_Annual_Grammy_Awards "63rd Annual Grammy Awards"), the album won the award, the first for James Taylor after being nominated in the same category in the [50th Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/50th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "50th Annual Grammy Awards") in 2008 for [James Taylor at Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor_at_Christmas "James Taylor at Christmas").

## Politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Taylor&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Politics")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/James_Taylor_receiving_his_National_Medal_of_Arts._%285492693444%29.jpg/250px-James_Taylor_receiving_his_National_Medal_of_Arts._%285492693444%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James_Taylor_receiving_his_National_Medal_of_Arts._(5492693444).jpg)

Taylor with U.S. President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") in 2011, preparing to be awarded the [National Medal of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Medal_of_Arts "National Medal of Arts")

Always visibly active in [environmental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_ecology "Political ecology") and liberal causes, in October 2004, Taylor joined the [Vote for Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vote_for_Change "Vote for Change") tour playing a series of concerts in American [swing states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_states "Swing states"). These concerts were organized by [MoveOn.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MoveOn.org "MoveOn.org") with the goal of mobilizing people to vote for [John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry "John Kerry") and against [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") in that year's presidential campaign. Taylor's appearances were joint performances with the [Dixie Chicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixie_Chicks "Dixie Chicks").

During October 19–21, 2008, Taylor performed a series of free concerts in five North Carolina cities in support of [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama")'s presidential bid.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-95)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-96) On Sunday, January 18, 2009, he performed at the [We Are One: The Obama Inaugural Celebration at the Lincoln Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We_Are_One:_The_Obama_Inaugural_Celebration_at_the_Lincoln_Memorial "We Are One: The Obama Inaugural Celebration at the Lincoln Memorial"), singing "Shower the People" with [John Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Legend "John Legend") and [Jennifer Nettles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Nettles "Jennifer Nettles") of [Sugarland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarland "Sugarland").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-97)

Taylor was active in support of Barack Obama's [2012 reelection campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama_presidential_campaign,_2012 "Barack Obama presidential campaign, 2012") and opened the [2012 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Democratic_National_Convention "2012 Democratic National Convention") singing three songs. He performed "[America the Beautiful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America_the_Beautiful "America the Beautiful")" at the President's [second inauguration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_inauguration_of_Barack_Obama "Second inauguration of Barack Obama").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-98)

Taylor performed multiple songs, including "America the Beautiful", "[Sweet Baby James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_Baby_James_(song) "Sweet Baby James (song)")", and "[You've Got a Friend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You've_Got_a_Friend "You've Got a Friend")" at a rally held by [Tim Walz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Walz "Tim Walz") on October 24, 2024, in [Wilmington, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmington,_North_Carolina "Wilmington, North Carolina"), as part of the [Kamala Harris 2024 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris_2024_presidential_campaign "Kamala Harris 2024 presidential campaign").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-99)

In December 2016, Taylor announced that he was canceling his scheduled February 2017 concert in Manila, Philippines. The decision was made in protest of the rising number of extrajudicial killings linked to the Philippine drug war under the administration of President [Rodrigo Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_Duterte "Rodrigo Duterte"). In a public statement, Taylor remarked that while he recognized the necessity of prosecuting the illegal drug trade, the reports of summary executions without judicial due process were "deeply concerning and unacceptable to anyone who loves the rule of law."[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-101)

Seven years later, following a change in the Philippine political administration, Taylor announced his return to the country. As part of his "An Evening with James Taylor & his All-Star Band" tour, he successfully performed a rescheduled concert on April 8, 2024, marking his first performance in the Philippines since 1994.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-102)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor#cite_note-103)

'''Judith Krantz''' (née '''Tarcher'''; January 9, 1928 – June 22, 2019) was an American magazine writer, fashion editor, and novelist. Her first novel ''[[Scruples (novel)|Scruples]]'' (1978) was a ''[[The New York Times Best Seller list|New York Times]]'' [[The New York Times Best Seller list|best-seller]]<ref>[http://www.hawes.com/1978/1978-06-18.pdf ''New York Times'' Best Seller List, 18 June 1978]</ref> and was translated into 50 languages. ''Scruples'', which describes the glamorous and affluent world of high fashion in [[Beverly Hills]], California, helped define a new sub-genre of the [[romance novel]] — the [[bonkbuster]] or "sex-and-shopping" novel.<ref name="bloom">{{cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-06-23/judith-krantz-novelist-who-mixed-sex-with-shopping-dies-at-91|title=Judith Krantz, Novelist Who Wrote Tales of Sex and Shopping, Dies at 91|newspaper=Bloomberg |date=June 23, 2019|access-date=June 24, 2019|via=www.bloomberg.com}}</ref> She also became a "celebrity author" through her extensive touring and promotion.<ref name="ham">[https://books.google.com/books?id=JEvyadBdwYQC&dq=Krantz+Scruples&pg=PT205 Hamilton, Jeff, Jones, Brian. ''Encyclopedia of American Popular Fiction'' (2010), p 199]</ref> Her later books included ''[[Princess Daisy (novel)|Princess Daisy]]'' (1980), ''[[Mistral's Daughter]]'' (1982) ''[[Till We Meet Again (novel)|Till We Meet Again]]'' (1988), ''Dazzle'' (1990), and ''Spring Collection'' (1996).<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2019/jun/27/judith-krantz-obituary|title=Judith Krantz obituary|last=Horwell|first=Veronica|date=June 27, 2019|work=The Guardian|access-date=July 2, 2019|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref>  Her autobiography, ''Sex and Shopping: The Confessions of a Nice Jewish Girl'', was published in 2000.<ref name="sex">[https://books.google.com/books?id=YnEpmAEACAAJ&q=Sex+and+Shopping:+The+Confessions ''Sex and Shopping: The Confessions of a Nice Jewish Girl'' (2000)]</ref>

==Biography==

===Early years===
Judith Bluma-Gittel Tarcher was born on January 9, 1928,<ref>{{cite news|url= https://www.upi.com/Top_News/2020/01/09/UPI-Almanac-for-Thursday-Jan-9-2020/6871578415895/|title= UPI Almanac for Thursday, Jan. 9, 2020|work= [[United Press International]] | date= January 9, 2020|access-date=January 16, 2020 |archive-date= January 15, 2020|archive-url= https://archive.today/20200115192229/https://www.upi.com/Top_News/2020/01/09/UPI-Almanac-for-Thursday-Jan-9-2020/6871578415895/|url-status=live|quote=…author Judith Krantz in 1928}}</ref> in [[New York City]], the daughter of Mary (Braeger), a [[Lithuanian Americans|Lithuanian-born]] attorney, and Jack D. Tarcher, an advertising executive.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/judith-krantz-dead-best-selling-author-journalist-dies-at-91-1220487|title=Judith Krantz, Best-Selling Author and Journalist, Dies at 91|website=The Hollywood Reporter|date=June 23, 2019 |access-date=June 24, 2019}}</ref> Her family was [[Jews|Jewish]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/06/23/us/judith-krantz-obit/index.html|title=Judith Krantz, romance novelist, dies at 91|first1=Leah|last1=Asmelash|first2=Melissa|last2=Gray|website=CNN|date=June 23, 2019 |access-date=June 24, 2019}}</ref> The "youngest, smartest, and shortest girl" in her year,<ref name="well">{{cite web| last =Ruark| first =Liz| title =Person of the Week: Judith Tarcher Krantz '48| publisher =Wellesley| date =February 12, 2001| url =http://www.wellesley.edu/Anniversary/krantz.html| access-date =February 6, 2007| url-status =dead| archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20060901234531/http://www.wellesley.edu/Anniversary/krantz.html| archive-date =September 1, 2006}}</ref> she graduated from the [[The Birch Wathen Lenox School|Birch Wathen School]] at age 16. Krantz then enrolled at [[Wellesley College]].

Krantz told ''[[The Boston Globe]]'' in 1982 that she attended Wellesley with three goals: to date, to read every novel in the library, and to graduate.<ref name="well" />  "Torchy", as her dormmates named her, held the dorm dating record as the only one to have 13 consecutive dates with 13 different men. Her grades were not as impressive as her extracurricular activities.<ref name="well"/> Krantz earned one A-plus in English, but had a B− average in her major and C average in everything else. Krantz had the opportunity to improve her marks when she took a short-story class during her sophomore year. Although the professor enjoyed her writing, he refused to give her an A because she had poor spelling, and he thought the B would teach her a lesson. Krantz claims to have learned the lesson well—she did not write fiction again for 31 years.<ref name="sex"/>

After graduating from Wellesley in 1948, Krantz moved to Paris, where she worked in fashion [[public relations]]. She enjoyed attending elegant parties, borrowing [[haute couture|couture]] gowns, and meeting prominent people such as [[Marlene Dietrich]], [[Orson Welles]] and [[Hubert de Givenchy]].<ref name="well" />

====Magazines====
The following year, Krantz returned to New York City, where began a career in magazine journalism. She worked in the fiction department at ''[[Good Housekeeping]]'' before being promoted to fashion editor and having the opportunity to write several articles for the magazine.<ref name="book">{{cite web| last =Huseby| first =Sandy| title =Judith Krantz: Life is even better than fiction| publisher =Book Page| year =2000| url =http://www.bookpage.com/0005bp/judith_krantz.html| access-date =February 6, 2007| url-status =dead| archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20070409061754/http://www.bookpage.com/0005bp/judith_krantz.html| archive-date =April 9, 2007}}</ref>

In 1953 Krantz attended a Fourth of July party hosted by her high school friend, [[Barbara Walters]]. There she met the future film and television producer [[Steve Krantz]].<ref name="steveobit" >
{{cite web  | last = Martin  | first =Douglas  | title =Steve Krantz, 83, Maker of TV Mini-Series, Dies   | work =New York Times
  | date =January 12, 2007  | url =https://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/12/obituaries/12krantz.html?ex=1326258000&en=f1844dbcdaa0605d&ei=5088&partner=rssnyt&emc=rss
  | access-date = February 6, 2007 }}</ref> The two were married the following year, on February 19, 1954. Three years later, she gave birth to their first son, and she gave up her full-time job, choosing instead to write part-time from home.<ref name="book" />  She wrote many freelance articles for ''[[Maclean's]]'', ''[[McCall's]]'', ''[[Ladies' Home Journal]]'', and ''[[Cosmopolitan (magazine)|Cosmopolitan]].''  Her best-known article was "The Myth of the Multiple Orgasm", which was published in ''Cosmopolitan.''<ref>Mansfield, Stephanie. [https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1986/05/20/steamy-sex-shop-talk-judith-krantz/cb92a7c2-91a5-4a43-9e8a-4292fbd1a83e/ 'Steamy Sex Shop Talk, Judith Krantz'], in ''The Washington Post,'' 20 May 1986</ref> Her magazine career gave Krantz an opportunity to interview many prominent women.<ref name="book"/>

===Novels===
In 1976, Krantz's husband decided to take flying lessons. Despite Krantz having a fear of flying, she joined the flying lessons with him,  after which her fears were subdued. Subsequently, she wrote fiction for the first time since college. Although her husband had been insisting for years that she was a natural storyteller, Krantz believed that she was writing the book simply to prove to him that she was not able to write good fiction.<ref name="steveobit"/>

She completed her first novel, ''[[Scruples (novel)|Scruples]]'', nine months later. The year it was published, 1978, Krantz turned 50. The books were not copyrighted under her own name but by Steve Krantz Productions.<ref name="steveobit"/> ''Scruples'' reached the number one spot on [[The New York Times Best Seller list|''The New York Times'' bestseller list]]. There were two sequels: ''Scruples Two'' (1992) and ''Lovers'' (1994).<ref name="ham"/>

Her second novel, ''[[Princess Daisy (novel)|Princess Daisy]]'', followed in 1980 and netted her $5 million before its publication. It also became a number one best seller, with the paperback rights selling for a then-record $3.2 million.<ref name="fraser">
{{cite web
  | last = Fraser  | first =C. Gerald  | title =Television Week  | work =New York Times  | date =November 6, 1983  | url =https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?sec=health&res=9903E4D61639F935A35752C1A965948260
  | access-date = February 6, 2007 }}</ref> It concerns the fabulously wealthy and glamorous Daisy, daughter of a Russian prince, who has to confront and overcome many harsh realities. The book is notable for having received one of the most scathing reviews ever written, by [[Clive James]].<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=London Review of Books|title=A Blizzard of Tiny Kisses|url=https://www.lrb.co.uk/v02/n11/clive-james/a-blizzard-of-tiny-kisses|last=James|first=Clive|date=5 June 1980|volume=2|issue=11}}</ref> Krantz continued her run of success with ''Mistral's Daughter'' (1982) (a multi-generational saga) and ''[[I'll Take Manhattan]]'' (1986), (about writer and socialite Maxi Amberville, a thinly disguised portrait of the author).<ref name="ham"/> Mistral's Daughter went beyond the formula (with only four sex scenes, all at the beginning of the book), delving into women's empowerment, art, Jewish spirituality, and the persecution of Jewish people in France during World War II.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Judith Krantz's MISTRAL'S DAUGHTER Revisited, Or If Judith Krantz Were a Man She'd Be Declared a Genius | last=Harlitz-Kern | first=Erika |url=https://ehkern.com/2022/01/14/judith-krantzs-mistrals-daughter-revisited-or-if-judith-krantz-were-a-man-shed-be-declared-a-genius/ | work=The Boomerang | date=January 14, 2022 |access-date=May 6, 2024}}</ref>   ''[[Till We Meet Again (novel)|Till We Meet Again]]'' (1988) which starts in the music halls of 1910s Paris and continues on until after the [[Second World War]], was the last to make the [[Publishers Weekly list of bestselling novels in the United States in the 1980s|annual top ten bestseller lists]], though the later novels continued to be popular.

''Spring Collection'' (1996) returns to the world of fashion, while ''The Jewels of Tessa Kent'' (1998) explores mother-daughter relationships; Krantz reportedly had a difficult relationship with her own mother.<ref>Shulevitz, Judith. '[https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2000/04/24/schmatte-hari Schmatte Hari]', in ''The New Yorker'', 16 April 2000</ref> She retired from writing that year at the age of 70, saying she had nothing left to say to her readers.<ref name="bloom"/> Over 80 million copies of her books are in print in over 50 languages. Seven of her novels have also been adapted for television (as either films or mini-series), with her husband having served as executive producer for some of them.<ref name="fraser"</> She also wrote one original mini-series for television, ''Judith Krantz's "Secrets"'', in 1992.<ref>[https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0146390/ ''Secrets, TV Mini-Series 1992''. IMDB]</ref>

===Family===
Krantz served on the advisory board of [[Compassion & Choices]], an organization dedicated to providing choices for the dying.<ref name="compassion">{{cite web
 |title=Advisory Board 
 |publisher=Compassion and Choices 
 |year=2005 
 |url=http://www.compassionandchoices.org/aboutus/advisor_board.php 
 |access-date=February 7, 2007 
 |url-status=dead 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080723131548/http://www.compassionandchoices.org/aboutus/advisor_board.php 
 |archive-date=July 23, 2008 
}}</ref> In 2006, she joined the Board of the [[Los Angeles Music Center]].<ref name="music" >
{{cite web  | title =Music Center Welcomes New Board Members   | publisher =Music Center  | date =October 24, 2006
  | url =http://www.musiccenter.org/102406.html  | access-date = February 6, 2007 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070927222455/http://www.musiccenter.org/102406.html <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date = September 27, 2007}}</ref>

Krantz's husband, Steve Krantz, died in 2007 of pneumonia. The couple had two sons, [[Tony Krantz]] and Nicholas Krantz, both of whom reside in the Los Angeles area.<ref name="steveobit" /> Krantz was the sister-in-law of children's entertainer and television host [[Shari Lewis]], who was married to Krantz's brother, [[TarcherPerigee|Jeremy P. Tarcher]], publisher of nonfiction books on health, psychology and New Age spirituality. Jeremy's daughter, Krantz's niece, is entertainer [[Mallory Lewis]]. Krantz has two grandchildren, Michael Krantz and Kate Krantz.

===Death===
Krantz died on June 22, 2019, at her home in the [[Bel Air, Los Angeles|Bel Air]] neighborhood of Los Angeles.<ref>{{cite news|url = https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/23/obituaries/judith-krantz-dead.html|title = Judith Krantz, Whose Tales of Sex and Shopping Sold Millions, Dies at 91|work = [[The New York Times]]|date = June 23, 2019|access-date = June 23, 2019|last = Fox|first = Margalit|author-link = Margalit Fox}}</ref>

Three years later, she gave birth to their first son, and she gave up her full-time job, choosing instead to write part-time from home.<ref name="book" />  She wrote many freelance articles for ''[[Maclean's]]'', ''[[McCall's]]'', ''[[Ladies' Home Journal]]'', and ''[[Cosmopolitan (magazine)|Cosmopolitan]].''  Her best-known article was "The Myth of the Multiple Orgasm", which was published in ''Cosmopolitan.''<ref>Mansfield, Stephanie. [https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1986/05/20/steamy-sex-shop-talk-judith-krantz/cb92a7c2-91a5-4a43-9e8a-4292fbd1a83e/ 'Steamy Sex Shop Talk, Judith Krantz'], in ''The Washington Post,'' 20 May 1986</ref> Her magazine career gave Krantz an opportunity to interview many prominent women.<ref name="book"/>

===Novels===
In 1976, Krantz's husband decided to take flying lessons. Despite Krantz having a fear of flying, she joined the flying lessons with him,  after which her fears were subdued. Subsequently, she wrote fiction for the first time since college. Although her husband had been insisting for years that she was a natural storyteller, Krantz believed that she was writing the book simply to prove to him that she was not able to write good fiction.<ref name="steveobit"/>

She completed her first novel, ''[[Scruples (novel)|Scruples]]'', nine months later. The year it was published, 1978, Krantz turned 50. The books were not copyrighted under her own name but by Steve Krantz Productions.<ref name="steveobit"/> ''Scruples'' reached the number one spot on [[The New York Times Best Seller list|''The New York Times'' bestseller list]]. There were two sequels: ''Scruples Two'' (1992) and ''Lovers'' (1994).<ref name="ham"/>

Her second novel, ''[[Princess Daisy (novel)|Princess Daisy]]'', followed in 1980 and netted her $5 million before its publication. It also became a number one best seller, with the paperback rights selling for a then-record $3.2 million.<ref name="fraser">
{{cite web
  | last = Fraser  | first =C. Gerald  | title =Television Week  | work =New York Times  | date =November 6, 1983  | url =https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?sec=health&res=9903E4D61639F935A35752C1A965948260
  | access-date = February 6, 2007 }}</ref> It concerns the fabulously wealthy and glamorous Daisy, daughter of a Russian prince, who has to confront and overcome many harsh realities. The book is notable for having received one of the most scathing reviews ever written, by [[Clive James]].<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=London Review of Books|title=A Blizzard of Tiny Kisses|url=https://www.lrb.co.uk/v02/n11/clive-james/a-blizzard-of-tiny-kisses|last=James|first=Clive|date=5 June 1980|volume=2|issue=11}}</ref> Krantz continued her run of success with ''Mistral's Daughter'' (1982) (a multi-generational saga) and ''[[I'll Take Manhattan]]'' (1986), (about writer and socialite Maxi Amberville, a thinly disguised portrait of the author).<ref name="ham"/> Mistral's Daughter went beyond the formula (with only four sex scenes, all at the beginning of the book), delving into women's empowerment, art, Jewish spirituality, and the persecution of Jewish people in France during World War II.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Judith Krantz's MISTRAL'S DAUGHTER Revisited, Or If Judith Krantz Were a Man She'd Be Declared a Genius | last=Harlitz-Kern | first=Erika |url=https://ehkern.com/2022/01/14/judith-krantzs-mistrals-daughter-revisited-or-if-judith-krantz-were-a-man-shed-be-declared-a-genius/ | work=The Boomerang | date=January 14, 2022 |access-date=May 6, 2024}}</ref>   ''[[Till We Meet Again (novel)|Till We Meet Again]]'' (1988) which starts in the music halls of 1910s Paris and continues on until after the [[Second World War]], was the last to make the [[Publishers Weekly list of bestselling novels in the United States in the 1980s|annual top ten bestseller lists]], though the later novels continued to be popular.

''Spring Collection'' (1996) returns to the world of fashion, while ''The Jewels of Tessa Kent'' (1998) explores mother-daughter relationships; Krantz reportedly had a difficult relationship with her own mother.<ref>Shulevitz, Judith. '[https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2000/04/24/schmatte-hari Schmatte Hari]', in ''The New Yorker'', 16 April 2000</ref> She retired from writing that year at the age of 70, saying she had nothing left to say to her readers.<ref name="bloom"/> Over 80 million copies of her books are in print in over 50 languages. Seven of her novels have also been adapted for television (as either films or mini-series), with her husband having served as executive producer for some of them.<ref name="fraser"</> She also wrote one original mini-series for television, ''Judith Krantz's "Secrets"'', in 1992.<ref>[https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0146390/ ''Secrets, TV Mini-Series 1992''. IMDB]</ref>

===Family===
Krantz served on the advisory board of [[Compassion & Choices]], an organization dedicated to providing choices for the dying.<ref name="compassion">{{cite web
 |title=Advisory Board 
 |publisher=Compassion and Choices 
 |year=2005 
 |url=http://www.compassionandchoices.org/aboutus/advisor_board.php 
 |access-date=February 7, 2007 
 |url-status=dead 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080723131548/http://www.compassionandchoices.org/aboutus/advisor_board.php 
 |archive-date=July 23, 2008 
}}</ref> In 2006, she joined the Board of the [[Los Angeles Music Center]].<ref name="music" >
{{cite web  | title =Music Center Welcomes New Board Members   | publisher =Music Center  | date =October 24, 2006
  | url =http://www.musiccenter.org/102406.html  | access-date = February 6, 2007 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070927222455/http://www.musiccenter.org/102406.html <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date = September 27, 2007}}</ref>

Krantz's husband, Steve Krantz, died in 2007 of pneumonia. The couple had two sons, [[Tony Krantz]] and Nicholas Krantz, both of whom reside in the Los Angeles area.<ref name="steveobit" /> Krantz was the sister-in-law of children's entertainer and television host [[Shari Lewis]], who was married to Krantz's brother, [[TarcherPerigee|Jeremy P. Tarcher]], publisher of nonfiction books on health, psychology and New Age spirituality. Jeremy's daughter, Krantz's niece, is entertainer [[Mallory Lewis]]. Krantz has two grandchildren, Michael Krantz and Kate Krantz.

===Death===
Krantz died on June 22, 2019, at her home in the [[Bel Air, Los Angeles|Bel Air]] neighborhood of Los Angeles.<ref>{{cite news|url = https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/23/obituaries/judith-krantz-dead.html|title = Judith Krantz, Whose Tales of Sex and Shopping Sold Millions, Dies at 91|work = [[The New York Times]]|date = June 23, 2019|access-date = June 23, 2019|last = Fox|first = Margalit|author-link = Margalit Fox}}</ref>
